hook.text: Processing speed peaks at twenty-five and slowly declines. But vocabulary keeps growing until seventy.

buildup.text: Fluid intelligence (raw problem solving) fades with age. Crystallized intelligence (knowledge) does not.

discovery.text: Older adults struggle with new tech but excel at judgment calls. Experience compensates for speed.

twist.text: Cognitive reserve—built through education, exercise, and social ties—can delay decline by years.

climax.text: The aging brain isn't just losing power. It's reorganizing—recruiting new regions to stay effective.

punchline.text: Older brains aren't weaker. They're different.

quiz.question: What type of intelligence keeps growing into old age?

details.summary: Cognitive aging involves declines in processing speed, working memory, and episodic memory, but crystallized intelligence, vocabulary, and wisdom often improve or remain stable into old age. The pattern is not uniform decline but a trade-off between fluid and crystallized abilities.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding cognitive aging combats stereotypes about old age. Many cognitive strengths peak later in life, and strategic compensations can offset declines.
takeaways: Processing speed and working memory decline with age
Vocabulary and crystallized knowledge remain stable or grow
Cognitive reserve and lifestyle factors influence the trajectory

faq.question: What is the difference between fluid and crystallized intelligence?
faq.answer: Fluid intelligence is the ability to reason about novel problems, and it declines with age. Crystallized intelligence is accumulated knowledge and vocabulary, which typically holds steady or increases into the seventies. Most real-world tasks rely on both types working together.

faq.question: Can cognitive decline be prevented?
faq.answer: Not entirely prevented, but lifestyle factors matter. Physical exercise, social engagement, cognitive stimulation, and managing cardiovascular health all contribute to cognitive reserve. Education and bilingualism may delay symptoms of decline. The brain remains more adaptable than once believed.
